title: Keep Only the Valid Integers
statement:
`int.Parse` throws on anything it cannot read as a 32-bit integer.
`int.TryParse` doesn't -- it hands back `true` or `false` and never raises,
which is exactly the shape a "keep the ones that work, skip the ones that
don't" filter needs, and exactly why wrapping `int.Parse` in a `try`/`catch`
for the same job is treating an ordinary, expected outcome (this token is
not a number) as if it were exceptional.

## Your function

```
public static List<int> ParseValidIntegers(List<string> tokens);
```

Return every element of `tokens` that parses as a valid 32-bit signed
integer, converted to `int`, in their original order. Tokens that do not
parse are simply left out -- not an error, not a `0` standing in for them.

## Watch out

- **`int.TryParse` tolerates leading and trailing whitespace** --
  `"  42  "` parses to `42`, not a rejection. Trimming the token yourself
  before calling `TryParse` is harmless but redundant; assuming whitespace
  needs handling by hand and rejecting it outright is not.
- **A value that overflows `int` fails to parse, even though every
  character in it is an ordinary digit.** `"2147483648"` -- one more than
  `int.MaxValue` -- is not a valid `int`, and `TryParse` correctly says so.
  `int.MinValue` itself, `"-2147483648"`, *is* valid; it is only the next
  value further out, on either end, that tips over.
- **`"3.5"`, `"0x1F"` and `"1e3"` are not valid `int` tokens.** `TryParse`
  (called without extra `NumberStyles`) only accepts an optional sign
  followed by decimal digits -- no decimal point, no hex prefix, no
  scientific notation. A regular expression built to "look like" what
  `TryParse` accepts is a second, separate implementation of a rule the
  method already enforces correctly; call `TryParse` and trust its answer.

tests.name: all valid tokens pass through unchanged
invalid tokens are dropped, not replaced with 0
whitespace around a token is tolerated, not a rejection
int.MinValue parses; one further out does not
int.MaxValue plus one overflows and is dropped
hex, scientific notation and decimals are all rejected
